title: Photovoltaic Inverters as Grid-Balancing Actuators: A Constraint-Stack Review of Controllability, Interoperability, and Aggregation
content: Photovoltaic inverters are the devices that actually change solar output on the distribution network, yet reviews of virtual power plants often treat them as abstract units that can simply be dispatched. This review therefore starts from the device. A solar system is controllable only when three things are true together: the inverter can change its behaviour, there is a way to send that change, and someone is allowed to send it. On the way up from the device, grid codes, communication choices, the path used to reach the inverter, and market rules each remove part of what the nameplate suggests. Four results follow from this view. First, inverters with the same rated power do not behave in the same way, and reactive-power support shortens inverter life. Second, standards agree on what a function means but not on how it is written in the message, so the cost of adding devices grows with the number of manufacturers. Third, choosing between a manufacturer cloud and a local controller is mainly a choice about who can still give orders when the link fails. Fourth, changing output when the network needs it keeps much more solar energy than a fixed capacity limit, but it does not replace network upgrades, the loss is not shared evenly, and a saved kilowatt-hour is not the same thing as avoided emissions. Overall, the tightest limits are interoperability, different national rules, reactive power that is required but not paid, and cybersecurity duties that are weaker than the control duties.
